note.explanation: Energetics studies the energy changes that occur during chemical reactions and physical changes. Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases energy. A reaction is exothermic when more energy is released in forming bonds than is absorbed in breaking them. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction.
examples: In an exothermic reaction, the energy released when new bonds form is greater than the energy needed to break the original bonds.
A burning match supplies activation energy to start the reaction between methane and oxygen.
note.simple: Think of bonds as needing energy to break and giving out energy when they form. Compare these two amounts to decide whether the overall change releases or absorbs energy.
note.checkQuestion: Does breaking a bond release energy or absorb energy?
note.title: Energy changes in reactions
steps: Identify which bonds break and which bonds form.
Add the energy absorbed to break the bonds.
Add the energy released when new bonds form.
For bond-energy calculations, use ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.
A negative ΔH means the reaction is exothermic; a positive ΔH means it is endothermic.
note.answer: The energy change depends on the difference between the energy absorbed in breaking bonds and the energy released in forming bonds.

mcqs.stem:
Q5.1. The following reaction is an exothermic reaction.

H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl

From where does the energy come to break the bonds of H₂ and Cl₂?
rationales: Molecular collisions are not the specified energy source for starting this reaction.
Sunlight supplies the energy needed to break the reactant bonds and initiate the reaction.
The surrounding is not the stated source of energy for this light-initiated reaction.
Collisions with the container walls do not provide the stated energy source.

mcqs.stem: Q5.2. Which of the following reactions has the least value of activation energy?
rationales: This reaction requires bonds in gaseous reactants to be broken before water forms.
Combustion of carbon requires sufficient energy to initiate reaction with oxygen.
The ions are already in solution and can react readily to form a precipitate, so this has the least activation energy.
This reaction requires energy to initiate reaction between hydrogen and solid iodine.

mcqs.stem: Q5.3. Formation of which hydrogen halide from the elements is an endothermic reaction?
rationales: Formation of HCl from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HF from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HBr from its elements is exothermic.
Formation of HI from its elements is endothermic.

mcqs.stem: Q5.4. What are the products of anaerobic respiration?
rationales: This includes carbon dioxide and water, but not the ethanol product given for anaerobic respiration in this question.
Carbon dioxide and water are not the products listed for anaerobic respiration here.
This is the correct set of products: ATP, ethanol and water.
This omits ATP, which is also a product.

mcqs.stem: Q5.6. What does it show when a chemical reaction is exothermic?
rationales: An exothermic reaction releases more energy when stronger new bonds form than it absorbs breaking the original bonds.
If the bonds broken were stronger than those formed, more energy would be absorbed than released.
The exothermic nature depends directly on the energy absorbed in bond breaking and released in bond formation.

mcqs.stem: Q5.7. When NaOH and HCl are mixed the temperature increases. The reaction is:
rationales: An increase in temperature indicates heat is released, not absorbed.
An endothermic reaction would not explain the observed temperature increase, and its enthalpy change would be positive.
The reaction is exothermic, but an exothermic reaction has a negative enthalpy change.
The temperature increase shows the reaction releases heat, and its enthalpy change is negative.

mcqs.stem: Q5.8. The average bond dissociation energy for the C-H bond is 412 kJ mol⁻¹. Which of the following process will have enthalpy change close to 412 kJ mol⁻¹?
rationales: This process breaks several bonds and forms hydrogen molecules, so its enthalpy is not the dissociation energy of one C-H bond.
This process involves several bond changes and formation of solid carbon, not just one C-H bond.
This process breaks all four C-H bonds in methane, so its enthalpy is much greater than one average bond energy.
This process breaks one C-H bond, so its enthalpy is close to the average C-H bond dissociation energy.

mcqs.stem:
Q5.9. The average bond energies for O - O and O = O are 146 and 496 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. Find the enthalpy in kJ for the following reaction?

H—O—O—H(g) → H—O—H(g) + 1/2 O=O(g)
rationales: The enthalpy is 146 − ½(496) = −102 kJ.
This has the wrong sign: the energy released in forming the O=O bond fragment is greater than the energy absorbed breaking the O—O bond.
This does not result from subtracting half the O=O bond energy from the O—O bond energy.
This does not use the reaction's half-mole amount of O=O correctly.

Q5.10. Why does the following exothermic reaction not occur?

C (Diamond) → C (Graphite)  ΔH= -3kJ mol⁻¹
rationales: The reaction's negative enthalpy change indicates graphite is energetically favoured, so this does not explain why the change does not occur readily.
This comparison does not explain the reaction's failure to proceed under ordinary conditions.
A high activation energy prevents the reaction from starting readily even though it is exothermic.
The difference in density does not explain why the reaction does not occur readily.

written.text: Q5.1. What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
written.finalAnswer: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure; enthalpy change is the difference between the enthalpy of products and reactants.

rubric.why: This identifies what enthalpy describes.
rubric.how: Describe enthalpy as the heat content of a system at constant pressure.

rubric.why: This distinguishes a change in enthalpy from enthalpy itself.
rubric.how: Give the difference between the enthalpy of products and reactants.

modelAnswer: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure.
Enthalpy change is the difference between the enthalpy of products and reactants.

written.text: Q5.2. Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?
written.finalAnswer: Energy must be absorbed to overcome the attractive forces holding the bonded atoms together.

rubric.why: Breaking a bond requires an input of energy.
rubric.how: Say that energy is absorbed.

rubric.why: This explains why energy input is needed.
rubric.how: Explain that energy overcomes the attraction holding the bonded atoms together.

modelAnswer: Energy must be absorbed to overcome the attractive forces holding the bonded atoms together.

written.text: Q5.5. What is the role of glycogen in our body?
written.finalAnswer: Glycogen is stored in the body as an energy reserve and can be broken down to glucose when energy is needed.

rubric.why: This identifies glycogen's storage role.
rubric.how: Say that glycogen is stored as an energy reserve.

rubric.why: This explains how the stored reserve is made available.
rubric.description: State how the body uses stored glycogen.
rubric.how: Explain that it can be broken down to glucose when energy is needed.

modelAnswer: Glycogen is stored in the body as an energy reserve.
It can be broken down to glucose when energy is needed.

written.text:
Q5.1. Physical changes which usually occur around us are given in the table. Write down whether they are exothermic or endothermic.

Conversion of hydrated salt into anhydrous salt; Conduction of electricity by metals; Burning of paper; Dissolving ammonium chloride in water; Vapourizing liquid nitrogen; Formation of rain from clouds; Evaporation of dry ice; Dissolving sodium carbonate in water.
written.finalAnswer: Conversion of hydrated salt into anhydrous salt: endothermic; conduction of electricity by metals: endothermic; burning of paper: exothermic; dissolving ammonium chloride in water: endothermic; vapourizing liquid nitrogen: endothermic; formation of rain from clouds: exothermic; evaporation of dry ice: endothermic; dissolving sodium carbonate in water: exothermic.

rubric.why: These changes require energy input.
rubric.how: Mark dehydration of hydrated salt, electricity conduction, ammonium chloride dissolving and liquid nitrogen vapourizing as endothermic.

rubric.why: These changes release energy.
rubric.how: Mark burning paper, rain formation and sodium carbonate dissolving as exothermic.

rubric.why: Evaporation requires energy to separate particles.
rubric.how: Identify evaporation of dry ice as endothermic.

rubric.why: The final response must classify all listed changes consistently.
rubric.how: Include both energy classifications and assign them to the correct changes.

modelAnswer: Conversion of hydrated salt into anhydrous salt: endothermic.
Conduction of electricity by metals: endothermic.
Burning of paper: exothermic.
Dissolving ammonium chloride in water: endothermic.
Vapourizing liquid nitrogen: endothermic.
Formation of rain from clouds: exothermic.
Evaporation of dry ice: endothermic.
Dissolving sodium carbonate in water: exothermic.

written.text: Q5.2. Explain why the reaction between atmospheric gases oxygen and nitrogen does not take place under normal conditions? But in the presence of lightning these gases react to give NO. The reaction stops as soon as the lightning stops.
written.finalAnswer: The reaction requires high activation energy because the nitrogen molecule has a strong triple bond. Under normal conditions the gases do not have enough energy to react. Lightning supplies the activation energy, and when it stops the gases no longer receive enough energy to continue reacting.

rubric.why: Activation energy explains why the gases do not react under normal conditions.
rubric.how: State that the reaction requires high activation energy.

rubric.why: The strong nitrogen bond helps explain the high energy requirement.
rubric.description: Explain the source of the high energy requirement.
rubric.how: Refer to the strong triple bond in nitrogen.

rubric.why: Lightning provides the energy needed to start the reaction.
rubric.how: Say that lightning supplies activation energy.

rubric.why: This explains why reaction ceases when the energy supply stops.
rubric.how: State that without lightning the gases are no longer supplied enough energy to react.

modelAnswer: The reaction requires high activation energy because the nitrogen molecule has a strong triple bond.
Under normal conditions the gases do not have enough energy to react.
Lightning supplies the activation energy and starts the reaction.
When the lightning stops, the gases no longer receive enough energy to continue reacting.

written.text: Q5.3. A reaction between natural gas (CH₄) and atmospheric oxygen does not take place when you mix them. As soon as you show a burning match stick, the reaction starts immediately and then it continues until one or both of the reactants is/are used up. Explain.
written.finalAnswer: Methane and oxygen need activation energy to react, so simply mixing them does not start the reaction. The burning match supplies this energy. The reaction is exothermic, and the heat released supplies energy for further reaction, so it continues until a reactant is used up.

rubric.why: This explains why mixing the gases alone does not initiate reaction.
rubric.how: State that methane and oxygen need activation energy.

rubric.why: This explains how the reaction is initiated.
rubric.how: Say that the burning match supplies the required energy.

rubric.why: The energy released by reaction sustains the process.
rubric.how: State that the reaction is exothermic and releases heat.

rubric.why: This explains why reaction proceeds until the available fuel or oxygen is consumed.
rubric.how: State that it continues until one or both reactants are used up.

modelAnswer: Methane and oxygen need activation energy to react, so simply mixing them does not start the reaction.
The burning match supplies this energy.
The reaction is exothermic and releases heat.
This heat supplies energy for further reaction, so it continues until one or both reactants are used up.

written.text:
Q5.1. Find out the enthalpy change of the following reaction using the given data.

N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol
Bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol
Bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol

rubric.why: The energy of all reactant bonds that break must be included.
rubric.how: Add 958.38 kJ mol⁻¹ and 498 kJ mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: This is the total energy absorbed in breaking the reactant bonds.
rubric.how: Obtain 1456.38 kJ mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: Two NO bonds form, so their energy contribution must be counted twice.
rubric.description: Find energy released in bond formation.
rubric.how: Use two NO bonds, giving 2 × 626 = 1252 kJ mol⁻¹ released.

rubric.why: Subtracting energy released from energy absorbed gives the reaction enthalpy change.
rubric.how: Calculate ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.

rubric.why: The positive result and unit are required for the final answer.
rubric.how: State the enthalpy change as +204.38 kJ mol⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Energy of bonds broken = 958.38 + 498 = 1456.38 kJ mol⁻¹.
Energy of bonds formed = 2 × 626 = 1252 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.

written.text: Q5.2. Explain the difference between the terms heat and enthalpy.
written.finalAnswer: Heat is energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference. Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure.

rubric.why: Heat describes energy in transfer, not energy stored as a property of the system.
rubric.how: Explain that heat is energy transferred between a system and surroundings.

rubric.why: A temperature difference is the reason heat flows.
rubric.how: Mention that transfer occurs because of a temperature difference.

rubric.why: This identifies enthalpy as a property of the system.
rubric.how: Describe enthalpy as the heat content of a system.

rubric.why: The constant-pressure condition distinguishes the enthalpy description used in reactions.
rubric.how: Include that enthalpy is considered at constant pressure.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference.
Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure.

written.text: Q5.3. Explain why formation of a bond is always an exothermic process.
written.finalAnswer: When atoms form a bond, attractive forces bring them into a more stable, lower-energy arrangement. The excess energy is released to the surroundings, so bond formation is exothermic.

rubric.why: Attraction between atoms is what allows a bond to form.
rubric.how: Mention the attractive forces between atoms.

rubric.why: Bonded atoms occupy a more stable, lower-energy state.
rubric.description: Compare the energy of the bonded state.
rubric.how: State that the bonded arrangement has lower energy or greater stability.

rubric.why: Release of energy is the defining energy change during bond formation.
rubric.how: Say that energy is released as the bond forms.

rubric.why: This is the required conclusion from energy release.
rubric.how: Conclude that bond formation is exothermic.

modelAnswer: When atoms form a bond, attractive forces bring them into a more stable, lower-energy arrangement.
The excess energy is released to the surroundings.
Therefore, bond formation is an exothermic process.

written.text: Q5.4. Explain the role of lipids in our body.
written.finalAnswer: Lipids store energy, form part of cell membranes, insulate the body and protect internal organs.

rubric.why: Lipids are an important energy reserve.
rubric.how: Mention that lipids store energy.

rubric.why: Lipids are a structural part of cell membranes.
rubric.how: Mention that lipids form part of cell membranes.

rubric.why: Insulation helps reduce heat loss.
rubric.how: Mention that body fat provides insulation.

rubric.why: Lipids also cushion and protect internal organs.
rubric.how: Mention that lipids protect or cushion internal organs.

modelAnswer: Lipids store energy.
They form part of cell membranes.
They insulate the body.
They protect internal organs.

written.text:
Q5.5. Explain the following terms.
Activation energy, Transition state, Aerobic respiration
written.finalAnswer: Activation energy is the minimum energy required to start a chemical reaction. A transition state is the short-lived, unstable arrangement of atoms at the highest-energy point during a reaction. Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water.

rubric.why: Activation energy is the energy barrier that must be reached for reaction to begin.
rubric.how: State that it is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction.

rubric.why: These features describe the temporary transition state.
rubric.how: Identify it as a short-lived, unstable arrangement of atoms.

rubric.why: The transition state lies at the energy maximum along the reaction pathway.
rubric.how: Say that the transition state is at the highest-energy point.

rubric.why: Oxygen is required for the process to be aerobic.
rubric.description: State the reactants or condition for aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Mention glucose breakdown in the presence of oxygen.

rubric.why: These are the products and energy output of aerobic respiration.
rubric.description: State the outcome of aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Name the released energy and the products carbon dioxide and water.

modelAnswer: Activation energy is the minimum energy required to start a chemical reaction.
A transition state is the short-lived, unstable arrangement of atoms at the highest-energy point during a reaction.
Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water.

written.text: Q5.1. Why is it essential to cook some of the food items while others we can eat without cooking?
written.finalAnswer: Cooking supplies energy that helps some food undergo the chemical changes needed to become edible, softer or easier to digest. Other foods are already safe and suitable to eat without this energy treatment.

rubric.why: Cooking supplies heat energy for changes in food.
rubric.how: Mention that cooking supplies heat or energy.

rubric.why: Energy enables changes that alter the food.
rubric.how: Explain that energy brings about changes in the food.

rubric.why: These are reasons some foods benefit from being cooked.
rubric.how: Mention improved safety, softness, edibility or ease of digestion.

rubric.why: This contrasts foods that do not need the cooking treatment.
rubric.description: Explain why some foods can be eaten uncooked.
rubric.how: State that some foods are already suitable to eat without cooking.

modelAnswer: Cooking supplies heat energy that helps some food undergo chemical changes.
These changes can make food edible, softer or easier to digest.
Some foods are already safe and suitable to eat without this energy treatment.

written.text: Q5.2. Why does fireworks look spectacular? What type of chemical compounds undergo chemical reactions during this activity?
written.finalAnswer: Fireworks look spectacular because their rapid exothermic reactions release heat, bright light, sound and coloured flames. The compounds that undergo these reactions include oxidizing agents and fuel compounds, along with metal salts that produce colours.

rubric.why: Rapid energy release makes the display energetic and bright.
rubric.how: State that fireworks reactions are rapid and exothermic.

rubric.why: Light is a main reason fireworks look spectacular.
rubric.how: Mention the bright light or coloured flames.

rubric.why: Oxidizing compounds help the fuel react rapidly.
rubric.how: Identify oxidizing agents as one type of compound.

rubric.why: Fuel compounds react and metal salts can produce coloured flames.
rubric.how: Mention fuel compounds and/or colour-producing metal salts.

modelAnswer: Fireworks look spectacular because their rapid exothermic reactions release heat, bright light, sound and coloured flames.
Oxidizing agents react with fuel compounds.
Metal salts produce the colours.

examTips: Short questions often ask for definitions or reasons, such as why bond breaking is endothermic; give the key energy idea directly.
For bond-energy calculations, show the energy of bonds broken, the energy of bonds formed, and then use ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed.
Include the correct sign and unit in enthalpy answers: a negative value is exothermic and a positive value is endothermic.
Reaction-profile questions test activation energy and relative energy levels; label the axes and the reactants, products and activation-energy barrier clearly.
For explanation questions about lightning or a match, connect the energy source to activation energy and explain whether released heat sustains the reaction.

explain.title: Enthalpy and enthalpy change
explain.body: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. Enthalpy change compares the enthalpy of the products with that of the reactants.

explain.title: Breaking and forming bonds
explain.body: Breaking a bond absorbs energy because energy is needed to separate the bonded atoms. Forming a bond releases energy as atoms move into a more stable arrangement.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic changes
explain.body: An exothermic change releases energy to its surroundings and has a negative enthalpy change. An endothermic change absorbs energy and has a positive enthalpy change.

explain.title: Activation energy and transition state
explain.body: Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction. At the top of the reaction pathway, the atoms pass through a short-lived, unstable transition state.

explain.title: Respiration and energy in the body
explain.body: Aerobic respiration releases energy when glucose reacts with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. Glycogen stores energy in the body, while lipids store energy and also help form membranes, insulate the body and protect organs.

mistakes: Do not say that breaking bonds releases energy; bond breaking absorbs energy.
Do not reverse the bond-energy calculation: use energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds formed.
Remember to count how many bonds form, and include the reaction coefficients.
Do not omit the sign or unit from an enthalpy answer.
Do not assume that every exothermic reaction starts immediately; a high activation energy can prevent it from happening readily.
Do not confuse heat, which is transferred, with enthalpy, which is a property describing the system's heat content.
